# Overview: The Whole Argument in Miniature

Everything in this research folder elaborates a single compact position. This
document states that position in ten theses. Each thesis gets a paragraph here
and a fuller treatment in the numbered documents.

## 1. S7 is functional OOP, and that changes what "class" means

S7 belongs to the generic-function tradition of object orientation (CLOS,
Dylan, Julia, S3, S4), not the message-passing tradition (Smalltalk, Java,
Python, R6). In this tradition a class answers the question *what is this
thing?* — its data, its invariants, its place in a dispatch hierarchy — while a
generic function answers *what can be done?* Methods belong to generics, not to
classes. This inversion is not cosmetic. It means behavior is organized around
verbs that many types can implement, extension happens by registering methods
from the outside, and "interface" is an implicit concept: a set of generics
that a class happens to support. Designing well in S7 means designing the
generic vocabulary with as much care as the class graph. See
[01-object-systems.qmd](01-object-systems.qmd).

## 2. Choosing the object system is a semantic decision, not a stylistic one

R offers S3, S4, S7, R6, environments, and vctrs, and the choice among them is
determined by the semantics of the thing being modeled. Domain values with
invariants and dispatch needs want S7. Homogeneous vectors that must slice,
recycle, and live in data frame columns want vctrs. Ongoing processes with
identity — sessions, connections, caches, accumulating conversations — want
reference semantics, which means R6 or an environment. Thin interoperability
veneers want S3. Real systems mix these deliberately: the most instructive
modern example is ellmer, where the mutable `Chat` is R6 and the immutable
`Turn`, `Content`, `Model`, and `Provider` objects it manages are S7. See
[01-object-systems.qmd](01-object-systems.qmd) and
[02-values-and-state.qmd](02-values-and-state.qmd).

## 3. Value semantics are the foundation; state is an opt-in at the edges

R's copy-on-modify physics makes S7 objects behave as immutable values:
"modifying" a property produces a new object. This is a strength to be
embraced, not a limitation to be engineered around. Values permit local
reasoning, cheap snapshots, honest testing, and freedom from defensive copying.
The architecture that follows is the functional core / imperative shell: pure
construction and transformation of domain values in the middle, and a thin
stateful rim — I/O, sessions, orchestration — around it. When invariants span
several properties, updates must be atomic (`S7::set_props()`), which is the
value-world analogue of a database transaction. See
[02-values-and-state.qmd](02-values-and-state.qmd).

## 4. Types carry meaning, not just shape

A string that holds an email address and a string that holds a layer id have
the same structure and entirely different meanings. Semantic types — the
newtype idea from statically typed languages — give meaning its own name and
its own laws. In S7 there are three carriers for this: a reused property
definition (cheapest), a class inheriting from a base type (nominal identity
while the value remains the primitive — ragnar's `MarkdownDocument` is a
character string with an origin), and a full composite class (when the concept
has internal structure). Sharing semantics rather than structure is also the
deep principle of loosely coupled integration: systems that agree on what data
*means* can evolve how it is *arranged* independently. See
[03-types-and-meaning.qmd](03-types-and-meaning.qmd).

## 5. Parse, don't validate — construction is the proof

Alexis King's slogan names the difference between a check that discards its
own result (validation) and a check that records it in a richer type
(parsing). In a dynamic language the translation is: boundary functions accept
loose input and return domain objects or fail loudly; from then on, possession
of the object *is* the evidence that its laws hold, and downstream code stops
re-asking. Constructors normalize; validators verify; nothing inside the core
ever touches raw wire input. The alternative — checks scattered through
processing code, each function distrusting its inputs — is what the language
security literature calls shotgun parsing, and it is both a correctness and a
clarity disaster. See [04-parse-dont-validate.qmd](04-parse-dont-validate.qmd).

## 6. Every invariant has exactly one home

Checking logic belongs on a ladder: external schema validators at the wire,
parsers at the boundary, property classes for type, property validators for
local laws, class validators for cross-property laws, aggregate-root
validators for cross-object laws, method preconditions for operation legality,
and internal assertions for developer invariants. Each rung may assume all
rungs below it and must not duplicate them. The most common validation design
failure is not a missing check but the same check living in four places,
drifting apart over time. See
[04-parse-dont-validate.qmd](04-parse-dont-validate.qmd).

## 7. Sum types deserve representation, and S7 gives you four encodings

Much of real-world modeling is alternatives: a source is vector *or* raster
*or* image; a message part is text *or* a tool call. Flag fields, clusters of
mutually exclusive nullables, and stringly typed mode switches are all sum
types begging for honest representation. S7 offers four encodings — subclass
families under an abstract parent, anonymous unions, enum-valued properties,
and discriminator-plus-validator hybrids — and choosing among them follows
from whether the variants differ in fields, in behavior, or only in value. The
notable loss relative to ML-family languages is exhaustiveness checking, which
must be recovered by convention and tests. See
[05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd](05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd).

## 8. Inherit for dispatch and substitutability; compose for structure

The classic warnings about inheritance — fragile base classes, implementation
coupling, a single rigid hierarchy axis — lose some force in functional OOP,
because an S7 parent contributes a property schema and a dispatch position
rather than a method table full of self-calls. But the discipline stands:
inheritance is for is-a relationships that dispatch exploits, shallow trees
with abstract roots and concrete leaves; composition is for has-a structure,
which is most structure. Inheriting merely to reuse field names is
schema cosplay. Interfaces — sets of generics with behavioral laws — are the
third mechanism, implicit in S7 and made explicit by s7contract. See
[05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd](05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd).

## 9. Documents are declarative programs; model them as object graphs, verify them at boundaries

A style, a config, a catalog, a query, a conversation transcript — these are
declarative programs interpreted by some engine elsewhere. The R package's job
is to be a good compiler front-end: construct lawful documents, enforce the
invariants that are cheap and local, and delegate full conformance to the
authoritative external validator at the wire. Schemas (JSON Schema, TypeScript
definitions, protobuf) are contracts and design inputs, not blueprints:
mirroring a schema one-interface-per-class imports its structure while
discarding the opportunity to encode meaning. Expression languages embedded in
documents deserve an escalation ladder — opaque passthrough, then constructor
combinators, then a typed AST — climbed only as far as analysis needs justify.
See [06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd](06-documents-schemas-dsls.qmd).

## 10. Abstractions must earn their keep

Every abstraction is indirection, and indirection has a comprehension price.
The layers that pay rent absorb a real axis of change: generic-to-method
absorbs behavioral variation across types; a semantic atom absorbs meaning
drift; a canonical spec projected into many artifacts absorbs representation
churn; a wire-name map absorbs serialization churn. Layers that do not pay —
pass-through wrappers, speculative interfaces with one implementation,
factories for shapes that occur once — should not exist yet. The practical
test is the rule of three: abstract after the pattern has recurred, not
before. The ecosystem itself demonstrates convergent evolution here: multiple
independent projects (s7x, rtemis's `PropertySpec` factories, and
property-factory layers in private codebases) grew nearly identical helper
strata over S7's deliberately minimal core, which is strong evidence for which
abstractions are genuinely load-bearing. See
[08-doctrine.qmd](08-doctrine.qmd).

---

The remaining documents unpack these theses with mechanics, examples from the
published ecosystem, and named anti-patterns. The doctrine document at the end
compresses everything back into decision guides you can apply in a design
review.
